source.title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data

page_placements.theme: Interpretability scores and explanations can be inflated, manipulated or unreliable

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests how automated explanation-simulation scores behave when evaluation-data construction cues are removed or controlled, and argues that scores on standard data can overstate evidence about explanations.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports fuzzing and detection results, but those do not directly test the claim versions about neuron interpretability or simulation scores on new text. It derives a matched-mark construction but does not build or score it. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: Most of the study concerns cues in the data used to score SAE-feature explanations. One part does bear on V7: Section 7 re-scores the explanations of 400 GPT-2 XL neurons from OpenAI's release. It uses GPT-4's published simulator, Jev and Llama-3.1-8B, and finds low pooled simulation scores (means 0.125–0.197, medians 0.099–0.169). A sequence-level oracle (η=0.288) beats all of them, so token-level skill is lower still. This reads as a restatement of how such scores should be interpreted (T5). The study does not set a 'good score' threshold or report what share of neurons clears one.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that automated-interpretability evaluation data carry the answer in their construction: explanation-free rules beat the stored LLM fuzzing scorers, and a sequence-order rule beats GPT-4's published simulator. Scores are higher on cued data, but the cues are not shown to reorder features. Benchmarks should report the best explanation-free rule, random-offset windows with the BOS token, matched marks and the within-sequence part of scores; on clean data a scorer can still show it reads the explanation. The paraphrase should add that on OpenAI's neurons a sequence-level oracle outscores both simulators, so pooled scores alone cannot show token-level skill.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates automated explanation-simulation scores and structural shortcuts in SAE-feature scoring data; it does not audit neuron poles or reproduce the Qwen3-32B job-share method.
record.method_sensitivity: Scores vary with the evaluation data: peak-centred stored crops versus random-offset natural windows, sequence order, and window length and composition. The study also compares simulation rubrics and scorer models.

fits_no_version.finding: For GPT-2 small SAE features, Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing items let a centre-token rule (0.979) and a mark-count rule (0.969) beat the stored LLM scorers (0.838). Simulation scores fall from 0.478 on stored snippets to 0.331 on random-offset natural windows, still well above the shuffled control (0.013).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Evaluation data for automated scoring of SAE-feature explanations contain construction cues that explanation-free rules exploit; scores must be reported beside such baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: On OpenAI's neuron release, predicting activity on the first five (top-activating) sequences scores 0.227, above GPT-4's 0.160. The post hoc rule exploits sequence order, which GPT-4 did not see.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-and-random simulation sets carry a sequence-membership cue that inflates pooled correlation scores.

record.code_released: The paper says code and related materials will be released upon publication; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The natural-window simulation results cover 49 features and one commercial scorer plus one open 8B simulator. The paper does not define a threshold for a good score or estimate the minority share. Neuronpedia marks are rebuilt using an inferred code version; the study says the matched-mark construction was derived but not tested. Its comparison of stored and natural windows also changes window length and composition.
record.rows_left_out: Fuzzing and detection outcomes in Sections 4-6 and Appendix G are not included because they do not directly test the listed claim versions about simulation scores on new text or neuron-pole interpretability. The paper's derived but unbuilt matched-mark design is not a reported scored result.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the SAE-feature rows to V7, but V7 concerns neuron explanations, so R1–R9 were relinked to none. Only the GPT-2 XL neuron analysis bears on V7, and its key new results (Jev, Llama and Laya on neurons) are not rows. The GPT-4 figure is the original source's own result, recomputed. No threshold or share of 'good' neurons is reported, so the 'minority' wording is supported only indirectly, through low means and medians.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job shares and the one-job, two-related-jobs, and not-understood proportions.
Interpretability shares across model families, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and scale up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization, and tool effects on neuron interpretability shares, including the InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error versus a trained replacement model.

Whether explanations written from activating examples fail to predict activation in the specific sense asserted; the paper evaluates simulation scores on new windows but does not establish that explanations fit their source examples and then fail on held-out activation cases.

The study does not define a threshold for a 'good' score or estimate the proportion of neurons meeting such a threshold; it tests one commercial scorer and one open 8B simulator on natural windows, not a broad set of stronger explainer models.

rows.operation_detail: Simulated token activations from explanations on natural-text windows and compared them with true activations using pooled Pearson correlation.

conditions.value: natural OpenWebText windows, random offsets; 49 features, 488 windows

rows.measure: Mean pooled Pearson correlation between simulated and true activations
rows.baseline: Shuffled explanation: 0.013; sequence-mean oracle: 0.166; per-feature offset oracle: 0.171
rows.uncertainty: 46 of 49 features above the shuffled-explanation result, p = 7.0 × 10−11; above per-feature offset oracle on 38 of 49, p = 1.4 × 10−4; above sequence-mean oracle on 34 of 49, p = 0.0094

rows.note: This is evidence that the scorer's predictions on these windows depend on the explanation and exceed the reported explanation-free references. The study does not define what score counts as 'good' or report the share of neurons meeting such a threshold.

relationships.condition: 400 GPT-2 XL MLP neurons with GPT-4's explanations, top-and-random sequences, simulators GPT-4 (published), Jev and Llama-3.1-8B
relationships.reason: Mean pooled r is low (GPT-4 0.160, median 0.099; Jev 0.197, median 0.169; Llama-8B 0.125), and a sequence-mean oracle (0.288) beats all three. Based on R10 plus Section 7 and Table 5 results not captured in rows (see missing).
relationships.display_finding: Mean pooled correlations were low with every simulator: 0.160 for GPT-4 (median 0.099), 0.197 for Jev (median 0.169) and 0.125 for Llama-8B. A sequence-mean oracle scored 0.288 and beat all three.

relation.reason: Section 7 re-scores 400 GPT-2 XL neuron explanations with three simulators, which bears on V7.

tranche.reason: Argues that simulation scores partly reflect sequence-level data structure (oracle 0.288 beats GPT-4 0.160), so the metric needs restating.

source_check.notes: The 0.160 GPT-4 score is recomputed from OpenAI's release (the original's data); Jev 0.197 and Llama-3.1-8B 0.125 are new runs on the same 400 neurons (88 Llama sequences dropped). No good-score threshold or share. Rows R1-R9 are GPT-2 small SAE features, not neurons. Jev's lead over GPT-4 is not detected in rank correlation.

statements.correction: Stored-crop vs natural-window fall (0.478 to 0.331) is Jev on 49 GPT-2 small SAE features; the sets also differ in window length (17 vs 64 tokens) and composition, so the cue is not isolated. eta 0.288 exceeds GPT-4 0.160, Jev 0.197 and Llama-3.1-8B 0.125 on OpenAI's 400 GPT-2 XL top-and-random sets; on natural windows Jev 0.331 exceeds eta 0.166. The paper concludes a pooled score alone cannot show token-level skill, and Jev's lead over GPT-4 is mostly between sequences. Scores still depend on the explanation: Jev with shuffled explanations drops to 0.017, and GPT-4 did not see sequence order.
statements.problem: Misreads the study in three ways. (1) The stored-vs-natural result comes from GPT-2 small SAE features, not neurons, and it is confounded. (2) The oracle beats the simulators only on OpenAI's sets. (3) 'Rather than the explanation' does not follow from the study.

statements.correction: Jev's mean simulation score on 49 GPT-2 small SAE features is 0.478 on stored peak-centred crops and 0.331 on random-offset natural windows (44 of 49 lower). Window length (17 vs 64 tokens) and composition differ between the sets and are not tested separately; 74-token stitched passages keep 0.476, a partial control for length only. Sequence order is a cue an explanation-free rule exploits on OpenAI's release (0.227, post hoc); GPT-4's simulator did not see the order. eta 0.288 vs GPT-4 0.160 on 400 GPT-2 XL neurons is right.
statements.problem: The neuron numbers are right. The first sentence misstates what varies: length and composition are confounds of the stored-vs-natural comparison, not tested factors. Simulator scores were not shown to vary with sequence order. The crop result is on SAE features.

statements.correction: The study tests whether evaluation data let explanation-free rules score without reading the explanation (structural shortcuts that confound or inflate scores). eta (0.288) is the ceiling only for rules constant within sequences, not a cap on simulator scores. All numbers given (0.160, median 0.099, 0.197, 0.125, 0.288, 0.227, 0.979, 0.969, 0.838) match the text.
statements.problem: The opening sentence ('tests whether the V7 metric itself caps scores') misdescribes the study, which tests for shortcuts that let rules score without the explanation. The numbers are right.
Minor: the 0.478 to 0.331 fall is for one scorer (Jev). That comparison also changes window length and composition.
